record.paper_title: Measurement of Energy Spectrum and Elemental Composition of PeV Cosmic Rays: Open Problems and Prospects
record.original_question: Where does the Galactic cosmic-ray spectrum end, and at what energy does the transition from Galactic to extragalactic cosmic rays occur, once the energy-dependent elemental composition through the knee and toward 10^17–10^19 eV is measured accurately?

evidence.quote: Determining elemental composition in the knee energy region is crucial to understand where Galactic CR spectrum ends and to give a solid basis to CR models up to the highest observed energies.

Indeed, it is widely believed that the bulk of CRs up to about 1017 eV are galactic, produced and accelerated by the shock waves of SuperNova Remnants (SNR) expanding shells [9], and that the transition to extra-galactic CRs occurs somewhere between 1017 and 1019 eV.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Cosmic rays (CRs) are high-energy charged particles observed at Earth with an all-particle differential energy spectrum that, on a log-log plot, is approximately a broken power law. Notable features include the "knee" near 3×10^15 eV (where the spectral index steepens) and the "ankle" near 5×10^18 eV (where it hardens again). It is generally accepted that CRs of sufficiently low energy are of Galactic origin (commonly attributed to diffusive shock acceleration in supernova remnant shells), while CRs at the highest energies are extragalactic. The elemental composition of CRs (the relative abundance of nuclei of different mass numbers A and charges Z) is energy dependent and is expected to evolve through the knee region and up to 10^17–10^19 eV.

Problem. Given accurate measurements of the energy-dependent elemental composition of the cosmic-ray flux through the knee region and across the energy interval 10^17 eV to 10^19 eV:

(a) Determine the energy E_end at which the Galactic component of the all-particle cosmic-ray spectrum effectively terminates (i.e., the energy above which the Galactic contribution becomes negligible compared with the extragalactic contribution).

(b) Determine the transition energy E_trans ∈ [10^17 eV, 10^19 eV] at which the cosmic-ray flux changes from being dominated by Galactic sources to being dominated by extragalactic sources, and characterize the shape of this transition (e.g., whether it is sharp or gradual, and the composition mix as a function of energy through the transition).
artifact.status_search_result: The location of the end of the Galactic cosmic-ray spectrum and the precise energy of the Galactic-to-extragalactic transition remain open problems in high-energy astroparticle physics. Recent measurements from KASCADE-Grande, IceCube/IceTop, Pierre Auger, Telescope Array, LHAASO, and TALE constrain composition trends but have not converged on a definitive transition energy; reviews continue to describe this as an outstanding question, with the transition believed to lie somewhere between ~10^17 and ~10^18.5 eV.

status_evidence.snippet: Composition-resolved spectra near the knee continue to be measured to clarify Galactic source contributions up to ~10^17 eV.
